title: Why You Should Handle Your Own Behavior Problems problems/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that sending misbehaving students to the office, though common, ultimately undermines a teacher's authority and makes classroom management harder in the long run. He explains that doing so signals to the class that the teacher is not the ultimate authority, emboldening difficult students to keep testing limits. Principals, he notes, lack the rapport, time, and management-plan structure to handle individual classroom incidents as effectively as the teacher who knows the students. Relying on the office instead pushes principals into using intimidation or persuasion, which he says is less effective than teacher-led accountability. He concludes that handling misbehavior directly, with calm and consistent enforcement of a classroom management plan, builds greater respect and strengthens the teacher's authority, while reserving office referrals for genuinely dangerous situations.
points: Sending students to the office signals to the whole class that the teacher isn't the ultimate authority, inviting more testing of limits.
Principals lack the rapport-building time and classroom-specific consequences that make teacher-led accountability effective.
Frequent office referrals correlate with more threatening, reminding, and pleading rather than firm follow-through.
Handling misbehavior directly strengthens a teacher's words and reinforces their classroom management plan.
Dangerous behavior like bullying or fighting is a legitimate exception that still requires administrator involvement.
quotes: But in the long run, sending students to the office makes managing your classroom more difficult. It also puts your administrator in the difficult position of trying to do for you what you can more effectively do yourself.
You see, when you send students to the office for misbehavior, you’re making a clear statement to your class that you’re not the ultimate authority of your classroom.
The more you send students to the office, the more you’ll find yourself threatening, giving reminders and chances, and trying to persuade and even plead for your students to behave.
They’re left with using their title and authority to try and convince or intimidate students into behaving for you.
Being seen as the leader and decision maker of your classroom will engender greater respect and admiration from your students.
No matter how easy it may seem in the moment, no matter how satisfying it may be to remove a student from your classroom, it’s a mistake to send students to the office.
